title: Making nonlinear dynamics look linear: Koopman lifts, snapshot fits (DMD) and low-dimensional modes (POD)
summary: A nonlinear system can sometimes be written exactly as a linear one in a bigger set of observables (a Koopman lift). Dynamic mode decomposition fits the best linear step map to snapshots by least squares, and proper orthogonal decomposition finds the few directions that carry most of the snapshot energy. Each is exact only when the chosen observables or modes are closed under the dynamics, so the honest check is a rollout from a new start.

source.note: Standard material (Koopman 1931 operator view, Schmid's DMD, POD by the singular value decomposition). The figure is the design system's synthetic F4.3 render of two trajectories and carries no project number. All numbers were computed for this page with NumPy and SciPy: a two-variable toy system, a damped rotation and a synthetic two-mode field.

read_the_figure.question: What does the state do over time, and is its motion described by one rule that could be written as a matrix acting on a state vector?
read_the_figure.axes: x: horizontal position in metres. y: height in metres. Arrows are the velocity, markers are at equal time steps, so the spacing of markers shows speed.
look_at: Whether markers bunch up (slow) or spread (fast): the speed is in the spacing as well as in the arrows.
Where the two curves separate: the drag term makes the motion nonlinear, and a linear model fitted on the early part would miss the divergence.
The shape of each curve: a straight line or a spiral can come from a linear rule, a curve that depends on position through products cannot.
Start and end points, which are the data a snapshot fit would use.
read_the_figure.proves: That the two systems differ in their trajectories from the same start. It does not show which equation produced them or whether a linear model of the state would fit.
if_wrong: Fitting a linear map to snapshots and judging it only on the data it was fitted to: the in-sample error can be tiny and the rollout from a new start wrong.
Equal marker spacing in time lost: speed cannot be read.
Calling a low-rank fit a model of the dynamics when only the shape of the data was captured.
must_check: A held-out start, not only the training trajectory.
Eigenvalues of the fitted map compared with the known or expected ones.
Singular value spectrum shown for any low-rank claim.

terms.meaning: A function of the state that we choose to track, such as the state itself, its square or a product of components.
The linear operator that advances every observable by one time step along the true dynamics; it acts on functions and is linear even when the dynamics are not.
Adding observables to the state until the evolution of the enlarged vector is linear.
The property that the time derivative of every tracked observable is again a combination of tracked observables. Without it the linear model is only an approximation.
Columns of states at consecutive times: X holds the first to the second to last, Y the second to the last.
The least-squares linear map A that carries each snapshot to the next; its eigenvalues give growth rates and frequencies.
The orthonormal directions, from the singular value decomposition of the snapshot matrix, that capture the most energy in a given number of modes.
The share of the total squared singular values carried by the first r modes.

remember: For a map $x_{k+1}=\Phi(x_k)$ the Koopman operator acts as $(\mathcal Kg)(x)=g(\Phi(x))$ and is linear in $g$.
If a finite set of observables is closed, the dynamics of the enlarged vector are exactly linear: $z_{k+1}=A\,z_k$.
DMD: $A=YX^{+}$ minimises $\|Y-AX\|_F$; for data from a linear system it returns the system's step matrix, with eigenvalues $e^{\lambda\Delta t}$.
A discrete eigenvalue $\mu$ gives the continuous rate $\lambda=\ln(\mu)/\Delta t$: its real part is the growth rate and its imaginary part the frequency.
POD by the SVD: the best rank-$r$ approximation has Frobenius error $\sqrt{\sigma_{r+1}^2+\sigma_{r+2}^2+\cdots}$ (Eckart-Young).
POD finds directions of large energy, not directions of important dynamics: a small, fast mode can matter more than its energy suggests.

understand.title: Easy: change the coordinates until the rule is a straight one
understand.text: Suppose the speed of a quantity depends on the square of another. Track the square as an extra variable: its own rule turns out to be simple. With the right extra variables the tangle becomes a set of independent decays that can each be solved on its own. A lift is the choice of those extra variables.

understand.title: Medium: DMD is a line fit for dynamics
understand.text: Write the snapshots as columns and ask for the matrix that best takes each column to the next. That is ordinary least squares. If the data came from a linear system with the observables you gave it, the answer is exact; if you gave it only part of the state, the answer is the best linear approximation, which can be poor. The eigenvalues are the modes' decay rates and frequencies. POD is a separate step: the SVD tells which directions the data live in, so the fit can be done in a handful of coordinates.

understand.title: Hard: closure is the whole question
understand.text: A lift is exact only if the derivatives of the chosen observables stay inside their span. For $\dot x=-x,\ \dot y=-2y+x^2$ the set $(x,y,x^2)$ closes because $\tfrac{d}{dt}x^2=-2x^2$. For a generic nonlinear system no finite set closes: one then truncates, and the error depends on how far the state wanders from where the data were taken. Eigenvalues of the fitted operator can also be spurious, so a rollout test from a new start is needed.

understand.title: Hardest: what linear models cannot do
understand.text: Linear models cannot represent several isolated fixed points or a limit cycle with an amplitude set by the nonlinearity in a finite lift; those need infinitely many observables or a nonlinear model. DMD fitted to noisy snapshots biases the eigenvalues towards faster decay. POD modes depend on the data set, not on the equation, and for transport-dominated flows converge slowly in the number of modes. The honest report is the rank, the energy captured, the rollout error from a held-out start and the eigenvalue comparison.

steps.title: Take a nonlinear toy system
steps.note: Two variables, a quadratic term. A linear fit of $(x,y)$ alone cannot reproduce it, because the $x^2$ cannot be written as a combination of $x$ and $y$. Atlas S22 and the Lotka-Volterra phase plane show nonlinear fields next to their linearisations.

steps.title: The lift closes
steps.note: Three observables and a linear system with eigenvalues $-1,-2,-2$. From $(x,y)=(1,0.5)$ the matrix-exponential solution matched a high-accuracy nonlinear integration to $4\times10^{-11}$ (computed), so the lift is exact, not approximate.

steps.title: DMD is least squares on snapshots
steps.note: Snapshots taken every 0.1 time units. The map $A$ is the step matrix of the data. Its eigenvalues $\mu$ translate to rates by $\lambda=\ln\mu/\Delta t$.

steps.title: Eigenvalues recover the rates when the lift is right
steps.note: DMD on the three lifted observables returned eigenvalues 0.9048, 0.8187 and 0.8187: the rates 1 and 2 (twice) to the printed digits (computed). DMD on $(x,y)$ alone returned 0.9048 and 0.8682, a wrong second rate (0.141 per unit time instead of 2).

steps.title: The test that matters: roll out from a new start
steps.note: Rolled out over the same 50 steps, the unlifted fit had an RMS error of 0.021 on the training start and 0.152 from a new start $(2,0)$, because the nonlinear term is larger there. The lifted fit had errors of $4\times10^{-12}$ and $4\times10^{-11}$ (computed). A good in-sample fit says little; the held-out start says what the model is worth.

steps.title: DMD on oscillations
steps.note: From 60 snapshots at $\Delta t=0.1$ the fit returned $\mu=0.9511\pm0.1928i$, which gives $\lambda=-0.3\pm2.0i$: decay rate 0.3 and angular frequency 2 recovered. A pair of complex eigenvalues is a damped oscillation; a single real one is a pure decay.

steps.title: POD: the energy in the leading modes
steps.note: For a synthetic field made of three spatial shapes (sin x, sin 2x, sin 3x) with different time behaviour, the singular values were 115.0, 28.1, 5.63 and 0 for the rest. One mode held 94.2 percent of the energy, two modes 99.8 percent (computed).

steps.title: Truncation error is known exactly
steps.note: For one mode the relative error was 0.2415 and for two modes 0.0475, equal to the square root of the discarded energy in both cases (computed). Three modes reproduced the field to rounding error, because the field was built from three. Energy is not importance: a small mode can still drive a rollout, so check the rollout, not only the spectrum.

worked.title: Fit and test a linear model of $\dot x=-x,\ \dot y=-2y+x^2$ from snapshots
worked.problem: Take snapshots of $(x,y)$ every $\Delta t=0.1$ from $(1,0.5)$ for $t\le5$. Fit DMD on $(x,y)$ and on $(x,y,x^2)$. Compare the eigenvalues with $e^{-0.1}$ and $e^{-0.2}$, and the rollout error from a new start $(2,0)$.

solution.text: Expected eigenvalues of the lifted system, whose rates are $-1,-2,-2$.
Fit on the lifted data: eigenvalues returned.
Fit on $(x,y)$ only: the second eigenvalue.
Rollout RMS error from the new start over 50 steps.

worked.answer: With the lift, DMD recovers the rates (eigenvalues 0.9048, 0.8187, 0.8187) and rolls out from a new start with error $4\times10^{-11}$. Without it, the second eigenvalue is 0.868, a rate of 1.41 instead of 2, and the rollout from the new start is off by 0.152. The lift supplied the missing observable $x^2$; the fit method was the same.

analyze.q: DMD on a damped oscillation returns an eigenvalue pair with modulus 0.95 at a time step of 0.1. What are the decay rate and the period (if the angle of the pair is 0.2 rad)?
analyze.hint: lambda = ln(mu)/dt; the angle over dt gives the angular frequency.

analyze.q: A POD with two modes captures 99 percent of the energy but a rollout in those two coordinates drifts away. List two reasons.
analyze.hint: Energy is not dynamics, and the projected dynamics may not be closed.

analyze.q: Why would DMD fitted on trajectories near a stable fixed point give a poor model far from it?
analyze.hint: Closure holds only on the region sampled.

evaluate.q: A report says our Koopman model has 99.9 percent accuracy. What numbers and plots do you want?
evaluate.hint: Held-out starts, rollout length, eigenvalues against the known ones, noise level, the rank used.

evaluate.q: When is a nonlinear model better than a large linear lift?
evaluate.hint: Limit cycles and several fixed points; number of observables; interpretability.

create: Pick a nonlinear system where a polynomial lift closes exactly (for example $\dot x=\mu x,\ \dot y=\lambda(y-x^2)$) and write its lifted matrix.
Design a test of how the DMD eigenvalues move when 5 percent noise is added to the snapshots, with enough repeats to see a bias.
Sketch the plot that shows POD energy and rollout error against the number of modes on the same axes.

checks.q: Why does the lift $(x,y,x^2)$ make the toy system linear?
checks.answer: Because $\tfrac{d}{dt}(x^2)=2x\dot x=-2x^2$: the derivative of the new observable is a multiple of itself, and $\dot y$ contains it linearly. The derivatives of all three observables lie in their span (closure), so the enlarged vector obeys $\dot z=Az$.

checks.q: DMD on a scalar decay sampled every 0.5 returns the number 0.6065. What rate is that?
The first POD mode holds 94 percent of the energy and the first two 99.8 percent. How large is the relative error of the rank-1 approximation?
checks.hint: Square root of the discarded fraction.
checks.answer: $\sqrt{1-0.9417}=0.2415$ (the energy fractions in the check were 0.9417 and 0.0561). The error is 24 percent although 94 percent of the energy is kept, because the energy is a squared quantity.

checks.q: A DMD fit reproduces its training trajectory to $10^{-12}$. Is the model good?
checks.answer: Not yet known. With enough observables or a long enough window a least-squares map can match its own training data exactly. In the check the unlifted fit had error 0.021 on its own start and 0.152 from a new start. Test on starts that were not used and compare eigenvalues with what is known of the system.

checks.q: You have 200 time snapshots of a field on 64 points. How do you build a 3-mode latent model from them?
checks.answer: Form the $64\times200$ matrix, take the SVD and keep the three leading modes $U_3$. Project to coefficients $a=U_3^{\top}x$. Fit DMD (or a small neural ODE) on the coefficients. Reconstruct with $U_3a$. Report the energy kept, the rollout error from held-out starts and the eigenvalues.
